text:
[EXECUTIVE SUMMARY]

The Annual National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2022/23 covers 1st July 2022 to 30th June 2023. It has been prepared in fulfilment of Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016, which require the COB to submit quarterly budget implementation reports for the National and County governments to Parliament.

The reporting period is primarily defined by a transition in government and recovery from the adverse effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. Upon taking office, the new administration instituted measures to rationalise expenditure on non-core activities, reduce deficit financing, and enhance funding for development activities. On the other hand, economic policies and programs that cushioned citizens and businesses from the adverse impact of the pandemic were sustained to build on the progress realised in returning the economy to a more sustainable growth path for improved livelihoods.

The revised gross budget for both National and County Governments for FY 2022/23 amounted to Kshs.4.18 trillion, comprising Kshs.3.67 trillion for the National Government and Kshs.515.18 billion for the forty-seven County Governments. The National Government budget consisted of Kshs.584.29 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.3.09 trillion for recurrent expenditure (Kshs.1.51 trillion for recurrent ministerial expenditure and Kshs.1.58 trillion for Consolidated Fund Services (CFS).

Receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.3.24 trillion, representing 89.6 per cent of the revised net estimates of Kshs.3.62 trillion. The Controller of Budget identified vital challenges that hindered effective budget implementation in FY 2022/23. They included: an increase in the public debt leading to a rise in the country's debt service costs, thereby limiting the government's fiscal space to undertake other critical policies and programmes; liquidity constraints arising from investors' preference for the shorter 91-day Treasury Bills; the establishment of a Special Committee on the verification of pending bills by the Cabinet on 27 th June 2023 did not include critical institutions in public finance management such as the Controller of Budget, Office of the Auditor General, the National Treasury and County Treasuries. Further, several MDAs' economic items and sub-programmes exceeded their allocated budget and reflected negative balances.

To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends a special audit of the existing loans and committed loans to link each loan to the funded project; the National Treasury should explore opportunities of accessing funding in multiple currencies to hedge against intense pressure on the local currency; fiscal consolidation to ensure budgetary discipline; consideration to include key players in public finance management in the pending bills verification committee as key stakeholders in the implementation of the budget; and finally, Accounting Officer should adhere to Section 43 of the PFM Act and ensure reallocated budget items are regularised in the consequent supplementary budget.

text:
[1  INTRODUCTION]

The Office of the Controller of Budget (OCoB) is an independent office established under Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya. Its primary mandate is to oversee the implementation of the budget for the National and County governments by authorising withdrawals from Public Funds under Articles 204, 206, and 207 of the Constitution and to report on the implementation of the budgets to each House of Parliament every four months. The report is in line with Section 9(5) of the COB Act 2016, which states that despite the first quarterly report of the year submitted under Section 9, each subsequent report shall contain cumulative amounts from the beginning of that year.

In the analysis of the budget performance, the MDAs are classified into ten sectors, according to the United Nations Classification of the Functions of the Government, including (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology, (iv) Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources, (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs, (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order, (vii) Health, (viii) National Security, (ix) Public Administration and International Relations, (x) Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation, sector.

[1  INTRODUCTION]

In the analysis of the budget performance, the MDAs are classified into ten sectors, according to the United Nations Classification of the Functions of the Government, including (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology, (iv) Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources, (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs, (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order, (vii) Health, (viii) National Security, (ix) Public Administration and International Relations, (x) Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation, sector.

The report is presented in six chapters. Chapter One is the introduction. Chapter Two presents receipts into the Consolidated Fund and actual withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund to fund expenditures for the Consolidated Fund Services, Development budget, Recurrent Budget and the equitable shareable revenue to County governments. The National government budget comprises gross and net estimates; the difference is referred to as Appropriation-In-Aid (A-I-A). A-I-A may be loans, grants from development partners and fees/levies for services rendered by MDAs and are used to defray expenses. Net Estimate is the proportion of budget funded through the exchequer by the National Treasury, and its performance is based on the proportion issued over the net estimates.

Chapter Three presents a summary of budget performance, the status of pending bills for the National and County governments, and MDAs' expenditure by economic classification disaggregated into development and recurrent votes. In addition, it presents Consolidated Fund Services performance, which includes Public debt, Salaries, allowances and Miscellaneous Services and Pensions and gratuity.

Chapter Three presents a summary of budget performance, the status of pending bills for the National and County governments, and MDAs' expenditure by economic classification disaggregated into development and recurrent votes. In addition, it presents Consolidated Fund Services performance, which includes Public debt, Salaries, allowances and Miscellaneous Services and Pensions and gratuity.

Chapter Four presents the budget performance of MDAs in each of the ten sectors. The absorption rate is the proportion of expenditure to the gross budget and expresses the implementation percentage of the budget in the financial year. The budget performance reflects the MDAs' expenditure, deliverables by programmes and sub-programmes, both financial and non-financial and major ongoing projects completion status.

Chapter Five presents the key issues identified by the Controller of Budget as inhibitors of effective budget implementation in FY 2022/23. Appropriate recommendations are included to address the problems identified.

Chapter Six provides the report's conclusion. Annexes support the chapters. text:
[2.2 Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund]

This section presents a summary of receipts into the Consolidated Fund for FY 2022/23. The Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and refers to the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the National government is paid. However, it excludes monies reasonably excluded by an Act of Parliament and payable into other public funds established for a specific purpose or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses.
heading_path: 2.2 Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

text:
[2.2.1   Revenue Estimates for FY 2022/23]

The original revenue estimate for FY 2022/23 was Kshs.3.54 trillion, revised to Kshs.3.61 trillion in Supplementary Budget I and to Kshs.3.62 trillion in Supplementary Budget II compared to Kshs.3.33 trillion (revised), allocated in FY 2021/22, representing 1.6 per cent growth (Kshs.0.06 billion). To finance the budget, the government budgeted to raise revenue from Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.08 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.65.56 billion), Domestic Borrowing (Kshs.948.11 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.513.42 billion) and Other Domestic Financing (Kshs.13.23 billion).

The specific revenue categories projected to grow were Tax Revenue by 0.4 per cent (Kshs.7.91 billion) and External Loans and Grants by 47 per cent (Kshs.164.09 billion). Non-Tax Revenue, Other Domestic Financing and Domestic borrowing reduced by 5.9 per cent (Kshs.4.1 billion) and 8.9 per cent (Kshs.92.35 billion), respectively.

The Equalisation Fund is established under Article 204 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that half a per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the National government each year, calculated based on the most recent audited revenue received, as approved by the National Assembly, to

text:
[4.1 Introduction]

MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nation Classification of Functions of Government, which is designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability. The chapter presents the performance of MDAs by sector in FY 2022/23 (see Annex III to Annex V, referenced on page 140 to page142). It provides budget allocations per sector detailing specific MDAs' exchequer issues, expenditures, and absorption on the budget. The chapter also presents the performance of MDAs' programmes and sub-programmes, key achievements and spending on development projects in FY 2022/23.

Sector performance is presented in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EI & ICT), (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance, Justice, Law, and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR) Sectors.

In FY 2022/23, the Education sector was allocated Kshs.568.22 billion (27.1 per cent of the total MDAs gross allocation of Kshs.2.09 trillion), recording the highest budget allocation while the GECA sector was allocated Kshs.29.08 billion (1.4 per cent), representing the lowest budgetary allocation. The allocation to the Education sector is skewed towards recurrent at Kshs.534.21 billion (94.0 per cent of the Sector's Budget) and development allocation of Kshs.34.02 billion (6.0 per cent of the Sector's Budget).

text:
[4.2.1  Introduction]

Agriculture is a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. It is a critical sector in the economic pillar of the Kenya Vision 2030.

The sector consists of six MDAs, namely: Ministry of Lands and Physical Planning, the State Department for Crop Development and Agricultural Research, the State Department for Livestock, the State Department for Fisheries, Aquaculture and the Blue Economy, the State Department for Cooperatives, and the National Land Commission (NLC), together with affiliated Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies and Training Institutions.

The overall goal of the sector is to attain National food and nutritional security and sustainable fisheries and land management, co-operatives growth, and the blue economy's utilization. Kenya's economic blueprint, the Kenya Vision 2030, and the Government Agenda on the 'Big Four' economic strategy both recognise the ARUD sector as a critical player in the economic and social development of the

N

A

country through food production, employment and wealth creation, foreign exchange earnings, security of land tenure and land management.
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

text:
[4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector]

The budgetary allocation to the ARUD sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.68.96 billion, revised to Kshs.98.68 billion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.94.16 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.68.90 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the ARUD sector represents 2.6 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.66.61 billion (70.7 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.27.55 billion (29.7 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Crop Development and Agricultural Research received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.49.42 billion (52.5 per cent of the ARUD sector's budget), while the National Land Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.1.48 billion (1.6 per cent of the ARUD Sector allocation).

The high allocation to the State Department for Crop Development and Agricultural Research is due to its vital role in increasing agricultural productivity and promoting market access and product development.

text:
[4.4.1  Introduction]

The Education Sector comprises six MDAs: The State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education, the State Department for University Education and Research, the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training, the State Department for Post-Training and Skills Development, the State Department for Implementation of Curriculum Reforms, and Teachers Service Commission (TSC) together with their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.

The Education sector is critical in promoting Kenya's political, social, and economic development by developing all-around individuals who can overcome prevailing societal challenges. The sector envisions attaining quality and inclusive education, training, and research for sustainable development. The Education sector is committed to providing quality education, training, science, technology, research, and skills development to all Kenyans.

The sector's overall goal is to increase access to education and training, improve the quality and relevance of education, reduce inequality, and leverage knowledge and skills in science, technology, and innovation for global competitiveness. The sector also envisions contributing to achieving the government agenda by providing the requisite skilled human resources and promoting research and development.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

text:
[4.4.2  Budget Performance for Education Sector]

The budgetary allocation to Education sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.544.52 billion, revised to Kshs.567.04 billion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.568.22 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.527.28 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the Education sector represents 15.5 per cent of the revised gross National budget. [4.6.1  Introduction]

The Environmental Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector (EPW&NR) comprises the Ministry of Environment and Forestry, the Ministry of Water, Sanitation and Irrigation, and the State Department for Wildlife.

The EPW&NR sector plays a critical role in Kenya's economy, securing, stewarding, and sustaining the environment and natural capital of the country. The overall goal of the EPW&NR sector is to ensure sustainable development in a clean and secure environment. The specific objectives include: providing the policy, the legal and integrated planning framework for sustainable management of the environment and natural resources for socio-economic development, enhancing good governance in the protection, restoration, conservation, development, and management of the environment, and forest resources for sustainable development, enhance control and development of water resources for sustainable social-economic development and to enhance water harvesting and storage for domestic, irrigation and industrial use. The sector also aims to increase land productivity through reclamation, rehabilitate degraded land through irrigation and drainage services, and enhance conversation of wildlife, biological resources, and their habitats for posterity.
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

[4.6.2  Budget Performance for EPW&NR Sector]

The annual budgetary allocation to the EPW&NR sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.107.18 billion, revised to Kshs.87.7 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.95.63 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to 102.12 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the EPW&NR sector represents 2.6 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.68.00 billion (71.1 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.27.63 billion (28.9 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The Ministry of Water and Sanitation and Irrigation received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.66.61 billion (69.6 per cent of the EPW&NR sector's budget), while the State Department for Irrigation had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.2.58 billion (2.7 per cent of the EPW&NR sector allocation). The high allocation to the Ministry of Water and Sanitation and Irrigation is due to its critical roles including increasing agricultural productivity through irrigation and drainage services; development of water and sewerage infrastructure; and increasing the availability of safe and adequate water.

During the FY 2022/23, two Votes were created during the budget revision under EPW&NR Sector i.e. the State Department for Irrigation with an allocation of Kshs.2.58 billion; and the State Department for Forestry with an allocation of Kshs.3.01 billion. The State Department for Irrigation purposes to attain universal access to adequate, safe and sustainably managed water resources, sanitation and irrigation. The State Department for Forestry is tasked with promoting and facilitating a clean healthy, safe and sustainably managed environment and natural resources.

[4.7.4  Key Achievements for the GECA Sector]

The State Department of East African Community (EAC) implemented several activities across the EAC integration pillars: EAC Customs Union, EAC Common Market, EAC Monetary Union and EAC Political Federation. The State Department for Regional and Northern Corridor Development completed public participation for the National Regional Development Strategy 2050. The Integrated Regional Development subprogramme completed the construction of the Total Mango Factory and processed 2.5 tonnes of mango puree against a target of 3 tonnes and 5 tonnes of mango juice against a target of 6 tonnes. The State Department of Trade improved fair trade and consumer protection by developing a trade remedies database. The Kenya Trade Remedies Agency finalised investigations, manuals, policies and procedures. The Agency developed four manuals, policies and procedures, thus achieving the target.

[4.8.1  Introduction]

The GJLO Sector consists of seventeen MDAs, which include the State Department for Interior and Citizen Services, the State Department for Correctional Services, State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services, National Police Service, State Department for Internal Security and National

N

A

Administration, the State Law Office and Department of Justice, The Judiciary, Ethics and AntiCorruption Commission (EACC), the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP), Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP), Witness Protection Agency (WPA), Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR), Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), Judicial Service Commission (JSC), National Police Service Commission (NPSC), National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC), and the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) as well as SAGAs and Tribunals under the Judiciary.

The GJLO Sector creates a favourable environment for the country's economic, social, and political development necessary for fulfilling the objectives of the Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages in peace and security building, correctional services, legal advisory services to government agencies, National government representation in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. The GJLO Sector also significantly promotes good governance, integrity, and corruption eradication, provides public prosecution services, regulates political parties, and protects witnesses and human rights. Further, the sector also delimits electoral boundaries and manages electoral processes, promoting gender equality, including marginalised groups and communities, and oversight of police operations.

Besides, GJLO Sector plays a role in border management, peace-building and conflict management, registration services, gaming industry regulation, population management services, eradicating drugs and substance abuse, crime research, and government printing services. The Sector also plays a crucial role in ensuring National values and promoting National cohesion.

[4.8.4  Key Achievements for the GJLO Sector]

In FY 2022/23, the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission received adequate support from the National Treasury to discharge its mandate. As a result, some significant achievements included completing 296 investigation files on corruption and economic crimes were forwarded to the Director of Public Prosecution. Further, they conducted 39 proactive covert investigations, averting possible loss of public funds estimated at Kshs.7.33 billion.

The Judiciary established operational instruments that enabled the operationalization of the Judiciary Fund. This aimed at ensuring financial independence to the Judiciary as envisaged by the Kenyan constitution. The Judiciary heard and determined the Presidential petition within the 14 days stipulated in the Constitution. Other petitions for Governors, Senators, Members of Parliament, and Members of the County Assembly are at various levels of the court. In addition, the Judiciary conducted admission of over 1000 Advocates, establishment of the first special Sexual and Gender Based Violence Court in Shanzu Law Court and operationalized six magistrate court Stations; Kenol, Rumuruti, Olkalou, Tinderet, Kabiyet and Madiany.

The National Police Service was created as a new vote effective 1st April 2023 and by the end of the financial 2022/23, it had procured new enhanced Medical Insurance Cover and Group Life Insurance Cover for all officers in the National Police Service.

The Independent Policing Oversight Authority continued its mandate of police accountability through various police operations, such as conducting investigations. As a result, they investigated and finalized 876 cases and made multiple recommendations, including prosecution and disciplinary action, in line with the Independent Policing Oversight Authority Act of 2011. Furthermore, the Authority conducted 762 inspections, monitored 122 police operations, and finalized the review and approval of IPOA Regulations to guide the implementation of the IPOA Act.

[4.9.4  Key Achievements for the Health Sector]

The Health Sector achievements for FY 2022/23 were based on the planned outputs and services to be delivered to the citizens per the budget allocations.

In the period under review, the preventive and promotive programmes identified 1.3 million people living with HIV and initiated antiretroviral treatment representing a coverage of 87 per cent. Under the same programme, Immunization coverage improved from 84 per cent in FY 2020/21 to 88 per cent in FY 2021/22 due to the procurement and installation of specialized vaccine storage equipment in over 3,500 health facilities and 290 sub-County vaccine depots.

The programme also distributed 16 million Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets across 27 Counties. This has benefited approximately 26 million persons and seen a drop in the prevalence of malaria infections from 8 per cent to 6 per cent. The sector also continued with the vitamin A supplementation programme for children ages 6 to 59 months. As of the close of FY 2022/23, they attained 86.3 per cent, surpassing the global and National target of 80 per cent.

The sector established 19 County-based cancer registries, an increase from 12 established in the FY 2020/21; 58 cancer treatment centres met the minimum standards of cancer centre care, 10 regional chemotherapy centres and three radiotherapy centres were fully established in Nakuru, Garissa, and Mombasa each being equipped with a state-of-the-art linear accelerator, Computed Tomography simulator and brachytherapy machine.

[5.1 Introduction]

This chapter highlights the critical issues that affected budget implementation in FY 2022/23 and provides recommendations for effective budget execution.
heading_path: 5.1 Introduction

text:
[5.2 Key Issues and Recommendations]

During the year, the Controller of Budget identified critical issues that affected budget implementation as discussed hereunder:
heading_path: 5.2 Key Issues and Recommendations

text:
[5.2.1  High Debt Services Costs]

As of 30th June 2023, the public debt stock stood at Ksh.10.25 trillion from Kshs.8.63 trillion reported on 30th June 2022. The National Treasury paid off Kshs.543.95 billion of loan principal, Kshs.607.28 billion as interest, Kshs.1.36 billion in commitment fees, and Kshs.536.85 million in penalties and other charges.

The country has a significant amount of public debt denominated in foreign currencies, which makes it vulnerable to currency fluctuations and exchange rate risks. The exchange rate between the Kenya Shilling and the US Dollar was roughly 117.87 Kenya shillings in July 2022, while in June 2023, it averaged 141.14, a difference of 23.27 shillings (approximately 18.9 per cent exchange rate depreciation). The depreciation of the Kenyan Shilling caused an increase in the debt stock and debt repayments (principal and interest) in Kenya Shilling terms. The continuous depreciation of the Kenya Shilling will necessitate an increase in the amount required for loan repayments. This will erode the government's fiscal space and limit the implementation of other critical policies and programs, resulting in budget adjustments.

The Controller of Budget recommends a special audit of existing and committed loans to link the loans with the projects funded through borrowed funds. Further, the office observed that the National Treasury has, over the years, acquired and absorbed loans on behalf of profitable Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies. These loans should be reviewed with the aim of transferring payment obligations to the Agencies.
heading_path: 5.2.1  High Debt Services Costs

text:
[5.2.2  Liquidity Constraints]

An analysis of domestic debt shows that investors preferred the shorter 91-day Treasury Bills, which is attributed to avoidance of duration risk. On several occasions, the Government could not raise adequate funds on the domestic market from Treasury Bonds, signaling an avoidance of long-term lending by investors.

Shorter-term maturity loans are more expensive and pressure revenue as a more significant proportions of the collected income is committed to debt servicing. The public debt payment is a first charge on the Consolidated Fund; and thus, inadequate collections from Treasury Bonds imply increased debt payments on Treasury Bill redemptions at the expense of the recurrent and development expenditures.

The Controller of Budget recommends fiscal consolidation to enhance fiscal discipline. Further, revenue measures, such as enhanced efficiency in tax administration to eliminate tax evasion, improve tax

N

A

compliance, widen the tax base and ensure government subsidies are aimed at supporting production for higher economic growth.
heading_path: 5.2.2  Liquidity Constraints

text:
[5.2.3  High level of Pending Bills]

As of 30th June 2023, the total pending bills of the National and County governments stood at Ksh.727.74 billion, consisting of Kshs.567.50 billion and Kshs.160.24billion for the National and County governments, respectively.

The Controller of Budget takes cognizance of the establishment of a Special Committee on the verification of pending bills by the Cabinet on 27th June 2023. The Committee was tasked with auditing liabilities for the period between 2005 and 2022 and consists of members from the Attorney General's Office, the State Department of Roads, the State Department of Public Works, the State Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority. The Committee, however does not include critical institutions in public finance management such as the Controller of Budget, Office of the Auditor General, the National Treasury and County Treasuries.

The Controller of Budget recommends consideration for the inclusion of crucial institutions in public finance management in the pending bills verification committee to enhance its effectiveness.
heading_path: 5.2.3  High level of Pending Bills

text:
[5.2.4  Reallocation of Funds]

Analysis of financial and non-financial reports submitted to the Controller of Budget shows that some MDAs' economic items and sub-programmes exceeded the budget and reflected negative balances and over-absorption of funds. Section 43 of the Public Finance Management Act specifies clear guidelines on budget reallocation.

The Controller of Budget recommends that Accounting Officers adhere to Section 43 of the PFM Act and ensure reallocated budget items are regularised in the consequent Supplementary Budget. For best practices, there is a need to identify budget lines and programmes/sub-programmes that are not likely to be utilised and reallocation to those likely to utilise the budget fully.

The Controller of Budget observed several challenges that hampered budget implementation in FY 2022/23. They include the rise in public debt service cost occasioned by the increase in the Country's public debt stock, liquidity constraints and an increase in pending bills.

To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends a special audit of the existing loans and committed loans, which will link the loans with the projects funded through borrowed funds; the National Treasury should also explore opportunities of accessing funding in multiple currencies to guard against intense pressure on the local currency. There is a need for fiscal consolidation with a target to reduce deficit budget financing and focus on tax administration measures to boost revenue collection.
